items.readable_text:
Content:
How can we find the diameter of a circle shown below?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e96b607af07cf020e6d1bbd261444064]

Content:
According to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. So, we must have

Content:
[MATH: m∠YVW|= (1)/(2) ⋅ mWY^(⌢); = (1)/(2) ⋅ 120^{∘}; = 60^{∘}.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: \triangle{VWY}] is inscribed in the circle and [MATH: \overline{VY}] is a diameter, we get that [MATH: m\angle{YWV} = 90^\circ] by Thales' theorem.

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \triangle{VWY}] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shorter side is [MATH: \overline{WV}=8\,\text{m},] and the hypotenuse is given by

Content:
[MATH: VY = 2 \cdot WV = 2 \cdot 8 = 16 \,\textrm{m}.]

Content:
Finally, we conclude that the diameter of the circle is [MATH: 16 \,\textrm{m}.]

items.title: Finding a Radius or Diameter of a Circle Given an Inscribed Special Right Triangle

sections.normalized_html: What is the radius of the circle above?
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/9b09715ed758e3594cc8b6c2f4992294]

What is the radius of the circle above?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc, we must have

[MATH: m∠ABC|= (1)/(2) ⋅ mAC^(⌢); = (1)/(2) ⋅ 60^{∘}; = 30^{∘}.]

Now, since [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] is inscribed in the circle and [MATH: \overline{BC}] is a diameter, we get that [MATH: m\angle{CAB} = 90^\circ.]

Hence, [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose longer side is [MATH: \overline{AB}.] Therefore, its hypotenuse is given by

[MATH: BC|= 2 ⋅ (AB)/(sqrt(3)); = 2 ⋅ (5)/(sqrt(3)); = (10)/(sqrt(3)); = (10)/(sqrt(3)) ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(sqrt(3)); = (10sqrt(3))/(3).]

Finally, the radius of the circle is [MATH: OB=\dfrac12\cdot BC = \dfrac{5\sqrt 3}{3} \,\textrm{cm}.]

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: m\angle{CAD}=105^\circ,] find the measure of [MATH: \angle{CBD}.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/79059d593b9e27b317c647f9a70160e9]

Given that [MATH: m\angle{CAD}=105^\circ,] find the measure of [MATH: \angle{CBD}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle{ADB}] and [MATH: \triangle{ACB}] are inscribed in the circle and [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter. Therefore,

[MATH: m\angle{ADB}=m\angle{ACB}=90^\circ.]

Now, the sum of the interior angles of the quadrilateral [MATH: {ACBD}] is

[MATH: 2 \cdot 180^\circ = 360^\circ.]

Therefore,

[MATH: m∠CAD + m∠C + m∠CBD + m∠D|= 360^{∘}; 105^{∘} + 90^{∘} + m∠CBD + 90^{∘}|= 360^{∘}; 285^{∘} + m∠CBD|= 360^{∘}; m∠CBD|= 75^{∘}.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Thales' theorem can be thought of as a consequence of the inscribed angle theorem.

Content:
Suppose that the points [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and [MATH: C] lie on the circumference of the circle where [MATH: \overline{AC}] is a diameter.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6a96420b1ac36ec02dd4fc376c54c1fb]

Content:
We wish to show that [MATH: m\angle{ABC}=90^\circ.]

Content:
First, since [MATH: \overline{AC}] is a diameter of the circle, the inscribed angle [MATH: \angle{ABC}] intercepts the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AC}.]

Content:
Moreover, [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AC} = 180^\circ] since it spans exactly half the circle.

Content:
According to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of the inscribed angle is always half the measure of its intercepted arc. Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: m\angle{ABC} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 180^\circ = 90^\circ.]

Content:
Hence, [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a right triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/991f245f46021114710b51f304c4b0ed]

[MATH: VY = 2 \cdot WV = 2 \cdot 8 = 16 \,\textrm{m}.]

Content:
Finally, we conclude that the diameter of the circle is [MATH: 16 \,\textrm{m}.]

Item 5 — Example: Finding an Angle in an Inscribed Quadrilateral

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Notice that [MATH: \triangle{ADB}] and [MATH: \triangle{ACB}] are inscribed in the circle and [MATH: \overline{AB}] is a diameter. Therefore,

[MATH: m\angle{ADB}=m\angle{ACB}=90^\circ.]

Now, the sum of the interior angles of the quadrilateral [MATH: {ACBD}] is

[MATH: 2 \cdot 180^\circ = 360^\circ.]

Therefore,

[MATH: m∠CAD + m∠C + m∠CBD + m∠D|= 360^{∘}; 105^{∘} + 90^{∘} + m∠CBD + 90^{∘}|= 360^{∘}; 285^{∘} + m∠CBD|= 360^{∘}; m∠CBD|= 75^{∘}.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Thales’ Theorem as a Consequence of the Inscribed Angle Theorem

Content:
Thales' theorem can be thought of as a consequence of the inscribed angle theorem.

Content:
Suppose that the points [MATH: A,] [MATH: B,] and [MATH: C] lie on the circumference of the circle where [MATH: \overline{AC}] is a diameter.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6a96420b1ac36ec02dd4fc376c54c1fb]

Content:
We wish to show that [MATH: m\angle{ABC}=90^\circ.]

Content:
First, since [MATH: \overline{AC}] is a diameter of the circle, the inscribed angle [MATH: \angle{ABC}] intercepts the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AC}.]

Content:
Moreover, [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{AC} = 180^\circ] since it spans exactly half the circle.

Content:
According to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of the inscribed angle is always half the measure of its intercepted arc. Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: m\angle{ABC} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 180^\circ = 90^\circ.]

Content:
Hence, [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a right triangle.
